# Abstract

Goal-directed remembering can be less affected by interference even as the same material becomes less likely to come to mind inadvertently.
The trauma-film paradigm examines this asymmetry in memory for distressing films: a visuospatial intervention task performed after a film reminder can reduce later intrusions while leaving voluntary memory relatively intact.
This selective interference effect is often interpreted through theories of traumatic memory in which intrusive and deliberate remembering depend on differently vulnerable memory representations.
Here we show that the same dissociation may follow from retrieved-context dynamics developed to explain episodic memory more generally.
We develop this account in an emotional Context Maintenance and Retrieval (eCMR) model that predicts sequences of film and non-film recall events.
The model links task items to film-associated context reinstated by a film reminder. 
That context can later cue task competitors as well as film items.
Unguided film recall declines when reminder-linked learning makes task items strong competitors.
Deliberate recall is less affected when a maintained film-category cue favors film candidates without equally supporting task competitors.
Recognition is less affected than recall because the model evaluates a presented candidate item's fit to context rather than selecting among film and task candidates.
This account clarifies when intrusive and voluntary remembering can diverge and situates selective interference within a broader computational theory of episodic learning and retrieval.

# Introduction

Traumatic experience foregrounds a tension between accessibility and selectivity in episodic memory.
From a functional perspective, events with lasting significance need to remain accessible in memory so remembered details can guide later decisions [@zhou2025episodic].
At the same time, adaptive retrieval is selective: what comes to mind should normally depend on current goals, cues, and circumstances.
Intrusive memories after trauma show how highly accessible event memories can strain the selectivity of retrieval.
In PTSD, such memories can come to mind unbidden and poorly matched to the present, causing distress and interfering with ongoing activity [@ehlers2000cognitive; @brewin2010intrusive; @krans2009intrusive; @iyadurai2019intrusive].
Explaining how episodic memory keeps consequential event memories accessible while regulating their retrieval is therefore a shared target for both clinical science and mechanistic theories of memory.

The trauma-film paradigm provides a controlled setting for comparing intrusive and voluntary memory for the same event [@holmes2008inducing; @james2016trauma].
Participants view distressing film material, record later intrusive memories of the film, and often complete voluntary-memory tests for the same material.
This design makes it possible to ask whether the same encoded event can remain accessible to deliberate retrieval while becoming more or less likely to come to mind involuntarily.
In such research, intrusion frequency is often only weakly related to voluntary-memory performance, such that the two measures dissociate [@holmes2004trauma; @james2016trauma].
The same encoded episode can therefore support both involuntary and deliberate remembering, and these modes can come apart empirically.

Visuospatial interference tasks make this dissociation experimentally sharper.
In immediate post-film studies, tasks such as Tetris can reduce later film intrusions while voluntary memory for the same material remains relatively intact [@holmes2009can; @holmes2010key; @deeprose2012imagery; @lau2019intrusive].
Delayed variants pair the interference task with a film reminder.
Participants return after roughly 24 hours to 3 days, view reminder cues for the film, and then complete Tetris.
This reminder-plus-Tetris sequence can reduce subsequent intrusions [@james2015computer; @kessler2020visuospatial].
The resulting pattern of reduced intrusions with relatively preserved deliberate memory is termed selective interference.
@fig-empirical-target defines the qualitative pattern targeted by the recall simulations: following a film reminder, the visuospatial task has a larger effect on unguided than deliberate film recall.

The selective interference effect has been used to argue that intrusive and voluntary remembering depend on differently vulnerable memory representations [@brewin1996dual; @brewin2014episodic].
Dual-representation accounts give this interpretation an architectural basis.
They link coherent deliberate recollection to hippocampally supported representations that bind event elements within a spatiotemporal context [@bird2012hippocampus; @bisby2020reduced].
Intrusive re-experiencing is linked more strongly to sensory and affective representations supported by amygdala and sensory systems [@brewin2010intrusive; @bisby2020reduced].
In immediate post-film interventions, visuospatial tasks are understood to compete for working-memory resources while sensory-perceptual imagery from the film is still being maintained and consolidated [@baddeley2000working].
Because later intrusions are assumed to arise especially from sensory-bound representations, the selective pattern is attributed to disrupting the representation most likely to support intrusions while leaving voluntary-memory performance relatively preserved [@holmes2009can; @holmes2010key; @deeprose2012imagery; @lau2019intrusive].
In delayed post-reminder interventions, the reminder is instead treated as reactivating the relevant memory before the task, allowing the interference procedure to alter later availability through reconsolidation or post-reactivation updating [@kindt2009beyond; @james2015computer].
Across these variants, selective interference is explained by treating the intervention as acting more strongly on sensory-bound, intrusion-supporting representations than on the contextualized representations proposed to support coherent deliberate recollection.

Here we argue that preserved voluntary memory does not, by itself, establish that a separate representation was spared. 
Selective interference can instead arise from differences in how film memories are cued and controlled at retrieval.
In the account developed below, a film reminder reinstates context associated with the film before task material is encoded.
Task material then becomes linked to that context.
When later remembering is guided by film-associated context, task and film material can therefore compete, interfering with film recall.
The task interferes less when retrieval depends less on context to access film material.
Deliberate recall can be less affected when a maintained film-category cue gives film candidates an additional source of support without equally supporting task competitors.
Tasks like recognition can also be less affected, because the test presents a candidate film item for judgment rather than requiring film material to be brought to mind.
On this account, the selective-interference effect emerges when retrieval conditions differ in how much they depend on film-associated context that also cues task material.

We formalize this retrieval account in an emotional variant [@talmi2019retrieved; @cohen2022memory] of the Context Maintenance and Retrieval (CMR) model [@polyn2009context].
Retrieved-context models treat context as a gradually changing state that is shaped by experience, reinstated by retrieval, and used to cue later memory search [@howard2002distributed; @sederberg2008context; @polyn2009context].
In CMR, items and context are linked by bidirectional associations.
Context cues candidate items, and retrieved items or items presented at test reinstate associated context [@polyn2009context; @polyn2009task].
Emotional CMR variants retain this item-context architecture while allowing emotional or source context to shape what is bound and later retrieved [@talmi2019retrieved; @cohen2022memory].
These properties make CMR a principled setting for a retrieved-context account of selective interference based on context reinstatement and item-context binding.
<!-- FIXME: In the Discussion, be more explicit about where CMR3 does not itself distinguish voluntary and involuntary retrieval. -->

Applied to the trauma-film paradigm, the model treats film, delay-period, task, and filler events as a continuous sequence through which context evolves.
A film reminder is implemented as item-to-context reinstatement before task encoding.
Later recall is implemented as context-to-item sampling from the film and non-film items supported by the current retrieval state.
When that context supports both film and task material, task items compete with film recall rather than merely weakening a film trace.

Deliberate recall is modeled with several retrieval-control processes.
Rather than universally producing the selective-interference pattern, we show that some control mechanisms increase film recall overall without substantially reducing the loss caused by task competitors linked to film-associated context.
In the simulations, the strongest protection comes from adding a maintained film-category cue that gives film candidates support not shared by task competitors.
This identifies a functional condition for selective interference: voluntary recall is protected when it depends less on film-associated temporal context that has also become supportive of task material.

The simulations follow a generalization-style modeling logic [@busemeyer2000model; @lohnas2023event].
Core parameters are anchored in an independent affective free-recall dataset [@dupertuys2026ukraine], and no trauma-film outcomes are fitted.
Simulation 1 varies reminder presence and effective task-context learning to test competitor formation.
Simulation 2 compares start-of-film context reinstatement, a maintained film-category cue, and retrieval monitoring to determine which control operations protect recall.
The recognition analysis tests how presenting a candidate film item for judgment changes where reminder-linked task competition enters retrieval.
Together, the simulations define a mechanistic alternative to selective-vulnerability accounts and identify conditions under which intrusive and voluntary remembering should appear more or less dissociated.

## Intentionality and Test Format in Selective Interference

Selective-interference studies are often described as comparing involuntary and deliberate memory, but the empirical contrast also depends on how each form of remembering is measured.
Diary measures count film memories after they inadvertently come to mind during daily life.
Laboratory intrusion tasks count film memories reported during a defined monitoring period, sometimes while film cues are present.
In both cases, participants report film memories when they occur without deliberately trying to recover film details.
Voluntary-memory tests differ in whether target film material must be recovered or is presented for judgment: free recall and specific-probe questions ask participants to bring film details to mind, whereas recognition asks participants to distinguish true from false film statements or film stills from lure images [@james2016trauma; @lau2019intrusive; @lau2021selectively].
Selective interference appears most consistent when intrusion reports are compared with recognition, and less uniform when film material must be brought to mind under more similar retrieval conditions.
@fig-empirical-examples illustrates variation in retrieval format across selected trauma-film studies [@james2015computer; @lau2019intrusive; @lau2021selectively; @mcconnell2026testing].

Comparisons between diary intrusion reports and recognition tests confound retrieval intentionality with retrieval format.
In immediate post-film Tetris studies, participants completed Tetris soon after film viewing and later reported fewer diary intrusions, while verbal or visual recognition remained similar across groups [@holmes2009can; @holmes2010key].
Delayed reminder-plus-Tetris studies used a later film reminder before Tetris and found a related pattern when diary or laboratory intrusion measures were paired with recognition [@james2015computer; @kessler2020visuospatial].
Later work pairing diary intrusions with recognition retained the same basic comparison [@asselbergs2024effectiveness].
In these studies, intrusion measures can count a film memory only after it comes to mind and is reported, whereas verbal and visual recognition tests present candidate film material for judgment [@lau2019intrusive; @lau2021selectively].
A reduction in intrusions with preserved recognition therefore does not, by itself, show that voluntary memory is preserved across retrieval formats.

Evidence is less consistent in designs that make intrusion and voluntary-memory measures more comparable.
Free recall and specific-probe questions make voluntary-memory performance depend on bringing film material to mind, matching a central requirement of intrusion reports [@lau2019intrusive].
Laboratory intrusion tasks collect reports during a defined period, making the setting more comparable to laboratory voluntary-memory tests than a week-long diary [@lau2019intrusive; @lau2021selectively].
Across matched recall and laboratory-report formats, effects of Tetris after a film reminder are less uniform.
Some designs still show reduced diary or laboratory intrusion reports with relatively preserved voluntary memory [@lau2019intrusive; @lau2021selectively].
A stricter matched-report design did not find the predicted reduction in involuntary memory [@mcconnell2026testing].

Variation across retrieval formats motivates a mechanistic account of when and why selective interference appears.
Recognition-based comparisons show selective interference more consistently.
The same comparisons confound retrieval intentionality with test format.
Attempts to compare recall-like measures across intentionality conditions are more methodologically robust, yet observe selective interference less consistently.
A complete account must therefore explain both how deliberate recall can remain preserved while unguided recall is reduced, as well as why selective interference depends on how retrieval is cued and measured.


# A Retrieved-Context Account of Selective Interference
